IGCSE Physics - Chapter 8: Electricity (25-32)

Question 25 (0625/41_Winter_2019_Q6) - Thermal Effects, Electricity

Fig. 6.1 shows a shower that takes in cold water. The water passes through an electric water heater and emerges from the showerhead at a higher temperature. The power of the heater is 9000 W.

(a) The shower is powered by a 230 V electricity supply.

(i) Calculate the current in the heater when it is switched or [2]

Tap to reveal answer
Using the formula P = VI, the current I = P⁄V.
I = 9000 W⁄230 V = 39 A.

(ii) Suggest a suitable rating for the fuse in the heater circuit. [1]

Tap to reveal answer
The fuse rating should be slightly higher than the normal operating current. A suitable rating would be 40 A.

(b) The specific heat capacity of water is 4200 J/(kg°C). The initial temperature of the cold water is 16°C. Determine the maximum mass of water that can be heated to a temperature of 35°C in 1.0s. [4]

Tap to reveal answer
First, calculate the energy supplied by the heater in 1.0s: E = Pt = 9000 W × 1.0 s = 9000 J.
Next, calculate the temperature change: ΔT = 35°C - 16°C = 19°C.
Using the formula E = mcΔT, rearrange to find mass: m = E⁄cΔT.
m = 9000 J⁄(4200 J/(kg°C) × 19°C) = 0.11 kg.

(c) A safety control in the shower switches off the shower when the water becomes dangerously hot. The control uses a thermocouple thermometer to measure the temperature of the heated water.

(i) Describe the structure of a thermocouple thermometer. Include a diagram in your answer. [2]

Tap to reveal answer
A thermocouple consists of two wires made from different metals, joined together at one end to form a junction (the sensing junction). The other ends of the wires are connected to a voltmeter. A voltage is produced which depends on the temperature of the junction.

(ii) Suggest one reason why a thermocouple thermometer is suitable for this purpose. [1]

Tap to reveal answer
A thermocouple is suitable because it has a very quick response time to temperature changes, which is essential for a safety device.
Question 26 (0625/41_Winter_2019_Q7) - Electricity

The resistance of a 1.0m length of resistance wire is 7.6Ω. A length of this wire is taped to a metre rule. A crocodile clip is connected to one end of the resistance wire exactly at the 0m mark of the rule. Fig. 7.1 shows the crocodile clip connected to terminal P. A second terminal Q is connected to a movable contact using a long length of connecting wire. The movable contact is in contact with the resistance wire at a length l from the 0m mark on the rule. The resistance R of the length l of the wire depends on l.

(a) On Fig. 7.2, sketch a graph to show how R varies with l for values of l between l=0 and l=1.0m. Mark appropriate values on the axes of the graph. [2]

(b) Fig. 7.3 shows a battery of electromotive force (e.m.f.) 12V connected across the 1.0m length of the resistance wire.

(i) State what is meant by electromotive force (e.m.f.). [2]

Tap to reveal answer
E.m.f. is the total energy supplied by a source (like a battery) per unit charge to drive the charge around a complete circuit.

(ii) Calculate:

1. the current in the resistance wire [2]

Tap to reveal answer
Using Ohm's Law, I = V⁄R. The full 12V is across the full 7.6Ω wire.
I = 12 V⁄7.6 Ω = 1.6 A.

2. the potential difference (p.d.) between terminal P and terminal Q when l = 0.35 m [1]

Tap to reveal answer
This setup acts as a potential divider. The potential difference is proportional to the length.
p.d. = (0.35 m⁄1.0 m) × 12 V = 4.2 V.

3. the charge that passes through the resistance wire in 5.5 minutes. [2]

Tap to reveal answer
First convert time to seconds: 5.5 minutes × 60 s/min = 330 s.
Using the formula Q = It.
Charge = 1.6 A × 330 s = 530 C.
Question 27 (0625/42_Winter_2019_Q7) - Electricity, Magnets And Currents

(a) Fig. 7.1 shows a coil of wire wound on a thin plastic cylinder. The plastic has no effect on any magnetic field. The galvanometer is extremely sensitive.

A magnet is fixed to a small trolley that runs without friction on a track through the cylinder and coil.

(i) The trolley is released from point A so it runs through the coil from right to left. State and explain what is observed on the galvanometer. [2]

Tap to reveal answer
A deflection is observed on the galvanometer, which then returns to zero and deflects in the opposite direction as the magnet leaves the coil. This happens because as the magnet moves through the coil, the magnetic field lines cut the coil, inducing an e.m.f. and causing a current to flow.

(ii) The trolley is now released from point B so it runs through the coil from right to left again. State what is observed on the galvanometer and explain why it is different to your answer in (a)(i). [2]

Tap to reveal answer
A larger deflection is observed. Releasing from point B, a greater height, means the trolley has a higher speed as it passes through the coil. This causes a larger rate of change of magnetic flux, which induces a larger e.m.f. and current.

(b) Fig. 7.2 shows an extension lead used to supply power to a 3kW electric heater on a cool evening.

State and explain three dangers with this arrangement. [4]

Tap to reveal answer
Danger 1: The extension lead is designed for a 25W lamp but is being used for a 3kW heater. The high current drawn by the heater will cause the thin wires in the lead to overheat, creating a fire risk.
Danger 2: There is a cut in the outer insulation of the lead. If the inner live wire is exposed, it creates a risk of electric shock.
Danger 3: The plug and socket are lying on damp grass. Water is a conductor, which can cause a short circuit or create a severe electrocution hazard.
Question 28 (0625/42_Winter_2019_Q8) - Electricity, Electron And Electronics

(a) A wire of length 2.0 m and cross-sectional area 0.40 mm² has a resistance of 0.14Ω. Calculate the resistance of another wire of the same material of length 3.0m and cross-sectional area 0.90 mm². [4]

Tap to reveal answer
Resistance R is proportional to length L and inversely proportional to cross-sectional area A (R ∝ L⁄A).
We can write the relationship as R₂ = R₁ × (L₂⁄L₁) × (A₁⁄A₂).
R₂ = 0.14 Ω × (3.0 m⁄2.0 m) × (0.40 mm²⁄0.90 mm²)
R₂ = 0.14 Ω × 1.5 × 0.444... = 0.093 Ω.

Question 29 (0625/43_Winter_2019_Q8) - Electricity

(a) Fig. 8.1 shows a negatively charged conducting sphere. On Fig. 8.1, draw the electric field pattern around the sphere. [2]

Tap to reveal answer
The electric field lines should be drawn as straight, radial lines that are evenly spaced. The arrows on the lines must point inwards, towards the center of the negative sphere.

(b) The current in an electrical device is 0.21A. Calculate the charge that flows during a 75 s period of time. [2]

Tap to reveal answer
Using the formula Charge (Q) = Current (I) × time (t).
Q = 0.21 A × 75 s = 16 C.
Question 30 (0625/42_Winter_2019_Q9) - Electricity

(a) Describe what is meant by the term electric field. [1]

Tap to reveal answer
An electric field is a region in space where an electric charge experiences a force.

(b) Fig. 9.1 shows two parallel conducting plates connected to a battery. On Fig. 9.1, draw five lines to show the electric field pattern between the two plates. [2]

(c) When fully charged, a 1.2V rechargeable battery can deliver a current of 210 mA for 10 hours.

(i) Calculate the charge that can be delivered by the fully charged battery. [3]

Tap to reveal answer
First, convert current and time to standard units.
Current = 210 mA = 0.21 A.
Time = 10 hours × 3600 s/hour = 36000 s.
Charge Q = It = 0.21 A × 36000 s = 7600 C.

(ii) Calculate the energy stored in the battery when fully charged. [2]

Tap to reveal answer
Using the formula Energy (E) = Voltage (V) × Charge (Q).
E = 1.2 V × 7600 C = 9100 J.

(iii) State the type of energy stored when the battery is charged. [1]

Tap to reveal answer
Chemical potential energy.
Question 31 (0625/43_Winter_2019_Q9) - Electricity, Electron And Electronics

Fig. 9.1 shows a circuit containing an LED and two resistors in parallel, each of resistance R. The normal operating voltage of the LED is 2.1 V and the normal current is 0.19A.

(a) (i) The potential difference (p.d.) across the LED is measured with a voltmeter. On Fig. 9.1, draw the symbol for this voltmeter connected to the circuit. [1]

(ii) The current in the LED is measured with an ammeter. On Fig. 9.1, draw the symbol for this ammeter connected to the circuit. [1]

(b) Calculate the value of R when the LED is operating normally. [5]

Tap to reveal answer
The circuit consists of the parallel resistor pair in series with the LED.
The total voltage is 3.7V. The voltage across the LED is 2.1V.
Therefore, the voltage across the parallel resistor pair is 3.7V - 2.1V = 1.6V.

The total current flowing through the series circuit is the same as the current in the LED, which is 0.19A.
The combined resistance of the parallel pair can be calculated using Ohm's Law:
Rparallel = V⁄I = 1.6V⁄0.19A = 8.42 Ω.

For two identical resistors R in parallel, the combined resistance is Rparallel = R⁄2.
So, R = 2 × Rparallel = 2 × 8.42 Ω = 17 Ω.
Question 32 (0625/41_Summer_2020_Q8) - Electricity

The power supply used in an electric vehicle contains 990 rechargeable cells each of electromotive force (e.m.f.) 1.2V. The cells are contained in packs in which all the cells are in series with each other. The e.m.f. of each pack is 54 V.

(a) Calculate the number of packs in the power supply. [2]

Tap to reveal answer
First, find the number of cells in one pack:
Number of cells per pack = e.m.f. of pack⁄e.m.f. of cell = 54 V⁄1.2 V = 45 cells.

Now, find the total number of packs:
Number of packs = Total number of cells⁄Cells per pack = 990⁄45 = 22 packs.

(b) When in use, each pack supplies a current of 3.5 A.

(i) Calculate the rate at which each cell is transferring chemical energy to electrical energy. [2]

Tap to reveal answer
The rate of energy transfer is power. For one cell, P = EI (using e.m.f. as it's the source).
Power = 1.2 V × 3.5 A = 4.2 W.

(ii) The packs are connected in parallel to supply a large current to drive the electric vehicle. Explain why it is necessary to use thick wires to carry this current. [3]

Tap to reveal answer
A large total current flows from the parallel packs. Thick wires have a smaller resistance. A lower resistance reduces the amount of thermal energy generated in the wires (since heat loss is proportional to I²R). This improves efficiency and prevents the wires from overheating or melting.
